questions.title: Design documents
questions.text: Describe what each of these design documents shows.

scheme.mark_scheme:
ERD: the entities / tables and the relationships (and their degree) between them (1)
Data dictionary: details of every field — name, data type, size, key, validation, description (1)
scheme.model_answer: ERD: the tables of the database and how they are related. Data dictionary: the name, data type, size, key and validation of every field.

questions.title: Order of design
questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

First the analyst identifies the [[1]] and their attributes from the requirements. Then the relationships are drawn in an [[2]]. Finally every field is described in the data [[3]].

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) entities (2) ERD (3) dictionary

questions.title: Entity or attribute
questions.text:
*A car-rental company records customers, cars and rentals. For each car it stores the registration number, model and daily price.*

Tick (✓) **one** box in each row.

scheme.mark_scheme: Customer entity (1); Daily price attribute (1); Rental entity (1); Model attribute (1)

questions.title: Relationships in a scenario
questions.text:
*In the car-rental company, a customer can rent many cars over time and a car is rented by many customers. Each rental is made by one customer for one car.*

State the degree of each relationship.

scheme.mark_scheme: Customer — Rental 1:M (1); Car — Rental 1:M (1); Customer — Car M:M (resolved by Rental) (1)
scheme.model_answer: Customer — Rental: one-to-many. Car — Rental: one-to-many. Customer — Car: many-to-many, resolved by Rental.

questions.title: Draw the rental ERD
questions.text: Draw the ERD for the car-rental company with the entities Customer, Car and Rental.

nodes.label:
Rental
RentalID, CustomerID, RegNo, StartDate, Days

scheme.mark_scheme: Correct connections (1); Customer 1 — M Rental (1); Car 1 — M Rental (1)

questions.title: Resolving M:M
questions.text: Explain why the Customer — Car relationship needs the Rental table in the database design.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Customer — Car is many-to-many, which cannot be implemented directly (1)
- Rental is a link table with both foreign keys, giving two 1:M relationships and storing rental details (1)
scheme.model_answer: Customers and cars have a many-to-many relationship, which a relational database cannot store directly, so Rental links them with CustomerID and RegNo as foreign keys and also records the dates.

questions.title: Data dictionary elements
questions.text: During the design phase of system development, a data dictionary is created. Name **two** elements that should be described in a data dictionary.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): the names of the fields / variables; their data types or formats; descriptions; validations; size of field; key field

questions.title: Data types for Rental
questions.text: Complete the data dictionary for the table `Rental` with the most suitable data type. Use **INT**, **VARCHAR**, **DATE**, **DECIMAL**, **BOOLEAN**.

scheme.mark_scheme: RegNo VARCHAR (1); StartDate DATE (1); Days INT (1); Deposit DECIMAL (1)

questions.title: Validation rules
questions.text: Suggest a suitable validation rule for each field of the `Rental` table.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Days (1): range, e.g. 1–30 / > 0
CustomerID (1): presence / must exist in Customer (lookup) / format
StartDate (1): presence / not in the past
scheme.model_answer: Days: range check 1–30. CustomerID: must exist in the Customer table. StartDate: presence check, not before today.

questions.title: Matching keys
questions.text: If `CustomerID` is VARCHAR(6) in Customer, it may be INT in Rental, because it is only a foreign key there.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: A foreign key must have the same data type and size as the primary key it refers to.

questions.title: Implement the design
questions.text: Write an SQL statement to create the table `Rental(RentalID, CustomerID, RegNo, StartDate, Days)` according to the design, with its primary key and two foreign keys.

scheme.mark_scheme:
CREATE TABLE Rental ( … ) (1)
fields with suitable types (1)
PRIMARY KEY (RentalID) (1)
FOREIGN KEY (CustomerID) REFERENCES Customer…, FOREIGN KEY (RegNo) REFERENCES Car… (1)
scheme.model_answer:
CREATE TABLE Rental (
  RentalID INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  CustomerID VARCHAR(6),
  RegNo VARCHAR(8),
  StartDate DATE,
  Days INT CHECK (Days > 0),
  FOREIGN KEY (CustomerID) REFERENCES Customer(CustomerID),
  FOREIGN KEY (RegNo) REFERENCES Car(RegNo)
);

questions.title: Checking a design
questions.text: State **two** checks the designer should make before the tables are created.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): all requirements / reports can be produced; tables normalised (3NF); every table has a primary key; relationships have foreign keys / M:M resolved; data types and validation suitable; sample data can be entered and joined
scheme.model_answer: 1 Every table has a primary key. 2 The tables are normalised to 3NF.

questions.title: A music school
questions.text: *A music school records students, teachers and lessons. Each lesson is for one student with one teacher in one room. A student has lessons with several teachers, and a teacher teaches many students.*

parts.title: ERD
parts.text: Draw the ERD for Student, Teacher, Room and Lesson.

scheme.mark_scheme: Lesson entity added (1); Student 1 — M Lesson (1); Teacher 1 — M Lesson (1); Room 1 — M Lesson (1)
scheme.model_answer: Student 1—M Lesson; Teacher 1—M Lesson; Room 1—M Lesson

parts.title: Data dictionary
parts.text: Complete the data dictionary entry for each field of `Lesson`.

scheme.mark_scheme: LessonID INT, PK (1); StudentID VARCHAR (same as Student), FK (1); LessonDate DATE, none (1)
scheme.model_answer: LessonID | INT | PK; StudentID | VARCHAR(5) | FK → Student; LessonDate | DATE | —

questions.title: A sports club — ERD
questions.text: *A sports club wants a database. Each **member** has a member number, name, phone and date of joining. Each **coach** has an ID, name and sport. Coaches run **training sessions**; each session has a date, time and maximum number of places and is run by one coach. Members **book** places on sessions; a member can book many sessions and a session has many members.*

parts.title: Entities
parts.text: Identify **two** entities and **two** attributes of one of them.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Entities: any two of Member, Coach, Session, Booking (1)
Attributes: two correct for one entity (1)
scheme.model_answer: Entities: Member, Coach. Attributes of Member: name, phone.

parts.title: Degrees
parts.text: State the degree of each relationship.

scheme.mark_scheme: Coach — Session 1:M (1); Member — Session M:M (1); link entity Booking with MemberNo and SessionID (1)
scheme.model_answer: Coach — Session: one-to-many. Member — Session: many-to-many, implemented with a Booking table containing MemberNo and SessionID.

parts.title: Draw the ERD
parts.text: Draw the entity-relationship diagram for the sports club database.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Entities Member, Coach, Session (1)
Booking link entity (1)
Coach 1 — M Session (1)
Member 1 — M Booking (1)
Session 1 — M Booking (1)
Accept answers with attributes / different relationship symbols.
scheme.model_answer: Coach 1 —— M Session 1 —— M Booking M —— 1 Member

questions.title: A sports club — data dictionary
questions.text:
The designer writes the data dictionary for the tables:

```text
Member  ( MemberNo, Name, Phone, JoinDate )
Booking ( BookingID, MemberNo, SessionID, Paid )
```

`MemberNo` looks like `M0251`.

parts.title: Data types
parts.text: Complete the data type for each field. Use **INT**, **VARCHAR**, **DATE**, **BOOLEAN**.

scheme.mark_scheme: MemberNo VARCHAR (1); Phone VARCHAR (1); JoinDate DATE (1); BookingID INT (1); Paid BOOLEAN (1)

parts.title: Validation
parts.text: Suggest a suitable validation rule for each field.

scheme.mark_scheme:
MemberNo (1): format M + 4 digits / unique / presence
Name (1): presence / length
JoinDate (1): presence / not in the future / range
scheme.model_answer: MemberNo: format check — M followed by 4 digits. Name: presence check. JoinDate: not later than today.

parts.title: Elements
parts.text: Name **two** other elements, apart from the data type and validation, that the data dictionary should describe.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): field name; size; key field; description; format; example

questions.title: Implementing the design
questions.text: The sports club design is now implemented in a DBMS.

parts.title: Matching keys
parts.text: Explain why `MemberNo` must have the same data type and size in `Member` and `Booking`.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- MemberNo in Booking is a foreign key referring to the primary key in Member (1)
- values must match to link / join the tables / referential integrity (1)
scheme.model_answer: In Booking, MemberNo is a foreign key that refers to the primary key of Member, so the values must be stored identically for the tables to be linked.

parts.title: CREATE TABLE
parts.text: Write an SQL statement to create the table `Booking ( BookingID, MemberNo, SessionID, Paid )` with its primary key and foreign keys.

scheme.mark_scheme:
CREATE TABLE Booking ( … ) (1)
fields with suitable types (1)
PRIMARY KEY (BookingID) (1)
FOREIGN KEY (MemberNo) REFERENCES Member, FOREIGN KEY (SessionID) REFERENCES Session (1)
scheme.model_answer:
CREATE TABLE Booking (
  BookingID INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  MemberNo VARCHAR(5),
  SessionID INT,
  Paid BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
  FOREIGN KEY (MemberNo) REFERENCES Member(MemberNo),
  FOREIGN KEY (SessionID) REFERENCES Session(SessionID)
);

parts.title: Why Booking
parts.text: Explain why the design needs the `Booking` table.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Member — Session is many-to-many, which cannot be implemented directly (1)
- Booking is a link table giving two 1:M relationships and storing booking details (Paid) (1)
scheme.model_answer: Members and sessions have a many-to-many relationship, which cannot be stored directly, so Booking links them and also records whether each booking is paid.

parts.title: Checks
parts.text: State **two** checks that should be made to confirm the design is correct.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): requirements can be met; normalised; primary keys; foreign keys / relationships; suitable types / validation; sample data test
scheme.model_answer: 1 Every report the club needs can be produced. 2 Sample bookings can be entered and joined to members and sessions.

summary: Designing the database for a new system — from the requirements to entities and relationships, drawing the ERD, resolving many-to-many relationships, and producing a complete data dictionary with data types, keys and validation for every table.

theory.title: Database design in the system life cycle

blocks.content: During the **design** stage of a new system, the analyst turns the **requirements specification** into a precise plan for the database. The two main design documents are:

items.title: Entity-relationship diagram (ERD)
items.content: Shows **which tables (entities)** the database has and **how they are related** (1:1, 1:M, M:M). It is the "map" of the database.

items.title: Data dictionary
items.content: Describes **every field of every table**: name, data type, size, key, validation, description and example. It is the "specification" that programmers use to build the tables.

blocks.content:
flowchart TB
  R[Requirements specification] --> E[Identify entities and attributes]
  E --> RL[Identify relationships and their degree]
  RL --> ERD[Draw the ERD and resolve M:M relationships]
  ERD --> N[Check the tables are normalised to 3NF]
  N --> DD[Write the data dictionary]
  DD --> SQL[Create the tables in the DBMS]
blocks.caption: From requirements to a working database

theory.title: Step 1 — Entities and attributes from the requirements

blocks.title: Case study — a music school
blocks.content:
*A music school wants a system to manage lessons. Each **student** has an ID, name, date of birth and parent's phone number. Each **teacher** has an ID, name and the instrument they teach. Every week a student has **lessons** with one or more teachers; for each lesson the school records the date, time, room and whether the student attended. Each **room** has a number and a capacity.*

| Entity | Attributes |
|---|---|
| Student | StudentID, FirstName, Surname, DateOfBirth, ParentPhone |
| Teacher | TeacherID, Name, Instrument |
| Room | RoomNo, Capacity |
| Lesson | LessonID, LessonDate, StartTime, Attended (+ links to student, teacher, room) |
**Nouns** in the requirements that have their **own data** (several attributes) and **many instances** are entities. Single values such as "date" or "instrument" are **attributes**.

blocks.title: Relationships in the music school
rows: A student has many lessons? Yes. A lesson is for many students? No (individual lessons)
A teacher gives many lessons? Yes. A lesson has many teachers? No
A room is used for many lessons? Yes. A lesson uses many rooms? No
A student has many teachers? Yes. A teacher has many students? Yes

blocks.content:
erDiagram
  STUDENT ||--o{ LESSON : attends
  TEACHER ||--o{ LESSON : teaches
  ROOM ||--o{ LESSON : "is used for"
blocks.caption: ERD of the music school database

blocks.title: Rules when drawing the ERD
items: One box per **entity**; name in the singular or plural, but consistently.
Connect related entities with a line; show the **degree** at each end (1 / M or crow's foot).
The **foreign key** goes in the table on the **"many"** side.
Replace each **M:M** relationship with a **link entity** (here *Lesson*), giving two **1:M** relationships.
Check that each table describes **one** entity and has a **primary key** (normalised to 3NF).

blocks.title: Data dictionary — Student
blocks.content:
| Field name | Data type | Size | Key | Validation | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| StudentID | VARCHAR | 5 | PK | Presence; format `S` + 4 digits; unique | Student number | S0107 |
| FirstName | VARCHAR | 30 | | Presence | First name | Dana |
| Surname | VARCHAR | 30 | | Presence | Family name | Seitova |
| DateOfBirth | DATE | — | | Range 2008-01-01 – 2020-12-31 | Date of birth | 2014-05-21 |
| ParentPhone | VARCHAR | 12 | | Length 12; format `+7` + 10 digits | Parent's phone | +77015554433 |

blocks.title: Data dictionary — Lesson
blocks.content:
| Field name | Data type | Size | Key | Validation | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| LessonID | INT | — | PK | Unique; auto-increment | Lesson number | 2381 |
| StudentID | VARCHAR | 5 | FK → Student | Must exist in Student | Who has the lesson | S0107 |
| TeacherID | VARCHAR | 4 | FK → Teacher | Must exist in Teacher | Who teaches | T012 |
| RoomNo | INT | — | FK → Room | Must exist in Room | Where | 14 |
| LessonDate | DATE | — | | Presence | Date of the lesson | 2026-10-12 |
| StartTime | TIME | — | | Range 08:00 – 20:00 | Start time | 15:30 |
| Attended | BOOLEAN | — | | True / False; default False | Did the student attend? | True |

A **foreign key** must have **exactly the same data type and size** as the primary key it refers to — `StudentID` is VARCHAR(5) in both Student and Lesson. Otherwise the tables cannot be joined and referential integrity cannot be enforced.

theory.title: Step 4 — From the design to SQL

blocks.content:
CREATE TABLE Student (
    StudentID   VARCHAR(5)  PRIMARY KEY,
    FirstName   VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    Surname     VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    DateOfBirth DATE,
    ParentPhone VARCHAR(12)
);
CREATE TABLE Teacher (
    TeacherID  VARCHAR(4)  PRIMARY KEY,
    Name       VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    Instrument VARCHAR(30)
);
CREATE TABLE Room (
    RoomNo   INT PRIMARY KEY,
    Capacity INT CHECK (Capacity > 0)
);
CREATE TABLE Lesson (
    LessonID   INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    StudentID  VARCHAR(5) NOT NULL,
    TeacherID  VARCHAR(4) NOT NULL,
    RoomNo     INT,
    LessonDate DATE NOT NULL,
    StartTime  TIME,
    Attended   BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
    FOREIGN KEY (StudentID) REFERENCES Student(StudentID),
    FOREIGN KEY (TeacherID) REFERENCES Teacher(TeacherID),
    FOREIGN KEY (RoomNo)    REFERENCES Room(RoomNo)
);
blocks.caption: The design implemented as tables

blocks.title: Checking the design
rows: Can every report and screen the client asked for be produced from these tables?
Is each fact stored once? No repeating groups, partial or transitive dependencies?
Does every table have a primary key? Is every relationship implemented with a foreign key?
Is every field's type suitable? Do validation rules prevent invalid data?
Can sample records be entered and joined correctly?

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Draw the ERD for the product supply management system (Stores, Products, Deliveries). [3]**
Entities defined (1); **Stores 1 — M Deliveries** (1); **Products 1 — M Deliveries** (1).

**Q: Name two elements that should be described in a data dictionary. [2]**
The **names of the fields** (1); their **data types / formats** (1). *(Also: descriptions, validation, field size, key field.)*

**Q: Complete the data dictionary entry for `LessonDate`. [2]**
Data type **DATE** (1); validation **presence check / not before the school year starts** (1).

- Leaving an **M:M** relationship in the ERD without a link entity.
- Choosing data types that do not fit the data (INT for phone numbers, VARCHAR for dates).
- A foreign key with a **different type or size** from its primary key.
- Validation that does not suit the field (a range check on a name).
- Designing tables that are not normalised (repeated customer data in every order).

items: What are the two main documents of database design?
From a short scenario, list the entities and their attributes.

Write a data dictionary for one of the tables.
